newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK democrats condemn China plan, plan petition.
newsitem.headline: HK democrats condemn China plan, plan petition.

text.p: Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp on Sunday condemned Beijing's plan to dilute civil liberties in the territory after it returns to Chinese rule this year and planned to petition Hong Kong's future leader.

"The Preparatory Committee's decision will restrict Hong Kong people's rights of freedom of speech, assembly, protesting and demonstrations," Democratic Party vice-chairman Yeung Sum said by telephone.

The 150-member China-appointed Preparatory Committee, which is overseeing Hong Kong's transition to mainland rule, on Saturday approved a Beijing plan to roll back civil liberties in the Special Administrative Region after China resumes control on July 1.
The proposal would amend the territory's Bill of Rights Ordinance and repeal a number of other laws allowing public protests and association with foreign political organisations.
Yeung said his party, which holds the most seats in Hong Kong's current elected Legislative Council, would introduce a motion in the legislature condemning the Preparatory Committee's decision.
He said they would also present a petition with more than 10,000 signatures to Chief Executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa on Tuesday.
Independent legislator Emily Lau urged Chinese leaders on Sunday to take a more "relaxed attitude", blaming China's moves to exert more control over Hong Kong on leadership wrangling in Beijing.
"With the post-Deng Xiaoping transition still in a state of flux, apparently there are no strong leaders in Beijing who dare to take a relaxed attitude," Lau told the Hong Kong government radio.
"Consequently, they all would rather err on the side of being over-cautious. Thus, they would have maximum control," she said.

Hong Kong will return to Chinese control on July 1, ending more than a century and a half of colonial rule. Beijing has promised Hong Kong that it will maintain a high degree of autonomy and keep its capitalist way of life intact for 50 years after the handover.
Lau also called on Tung to "learn to speak for the Hong Kong people rather than to be just a mouthpiece of Beijing".
The Preparatory Committee's proposal will now go to China's National People's Congress, or parliament, for ratification.
An opinion survey published on Sunday found most Hong Kong people appear to be against China's plan to roll back civil liberties.
The telephone poll, by the independent watchdog Hong Kong Policy Viewers, found 54.8 percent of 573 respondents were against Beijing's proposal, survey organisers said.
